analysis.one_liner: Lets FEMA take over buying and distributing medical supplies during emergencies when prices spike more than 15% above normal.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced by one senator with no cosponsors in June 2020, it sat in committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During a declared national health emergency, the bill would have made the Federal Emergency Management Agency the sole federal buyer, owner, and distributor of key medical supplies — N95 masks, ventilators, gloves, gowns, tests — whenever the market price was more than 15% above the prior year's average. FEMA would contract directly with manufacturers, set the resale price for states and others, and replenish the Strategic National Stockpile afterward. It also would have created a joint congressional committee to oversee emergency defense production.
analysis.who_benefits: States, hospitals, and ordinary people who need protective gear and ventilators during a pandemic or bioterror attack. Federal buying at fair prices and organized distribution would replace the scramble in which states bid against each other and against the federal government, driving prices up.

how_it_helps.text: In a covered emergency, FEMA becomes the sole owner and distributor of federally obtained medical equipment whose price exceeds the prior year's fair market price by more than 15%, replacing a bidding war with a single federal buyer at a set price [S2][S3].

FEMA must contract with all persons capable of producing the equipment, and those contracts supersede existing ones, directing manufacturing capacity toward the emergency and toward refilling the Strategic National Stockpile afterward [S3].

States — including territories and Indian tribes — and individuals can request allocations, with distribution guided by caseload and need, and FEMA must report to Congress every two weeks on what was distributed and where [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Medical supply manufacturers and distributors lose the ability to sell scarce masks, ventilators, and gloves at emergency prices above 15% of the prior year's average, and federal contracts would displace their existing sales contracts.

drawbacks.text: The bill concentrates enormous power in FEMA, an agency built for natural disasters rather than public health, to set prices and force contracts that supersede private agreements, raising the risk of mismanaged or politically steered procurement [S3].

Requiring contracts with all persons capable of producing equipment, without a liability shield or compensation terms spelled out, could deter manufacturers from participating or invite legal disputes over the supersession of existing contracts [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The problem it targets was real and visible in 2020: states bid against each other for masks and ventilators while prices spiked, and the federal stockpile ran short. Centralizing federal buying could fix that, but the design is crude — it hands FEMA sweeping authority on price-setting and contract supersession without many guardrails, and it was written as a single-senator proposal rather than a negotiated bill. The core idea had merit; the details would have needed substantial work.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2020 with no cosponsors, referred to the Senate Homeland Security Committee, and never taken up before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Warren introduced the bill on June 1, 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs [S1][S5].
No cosponsors signed on [S4], and the action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor action after the referral [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so the bill died in committee without a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medical equipment suppliers and distributors kept the emergency-era system intact, in which scarcity prices could run far above normal and the federal government competed with states for supplies. No committee or senator had to take a public position.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medical supply sellers who kept scarcity pricing

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or recorded opposition exist; the bill never advanced past referral and drew zero cosponsors [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Medical equipment manufacturers and distributors (N95 respirators, ventilators, gloves, gowns, tests)
industries.note: The bill would strip the right to sell scarce supplies at more than 15% above the prior year's price during a declared emergency and would override existing contracts with federal ones. During the 2020 pandemic this is precisely the margin suppliers captured while states bid against each other.
